extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent agents, patent lawyers, and law students (United Kingdom practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on interpreting patent specifications and claims, and on the statutory procedure, grounds, and practice for opposing the grant of patents (UK, Acts of 1883/1888 era). Covers timing, evidence, appeals, costs, priority, mala fides, and patent date/duration rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of claims with reference to the whole specification
rubrics_metrics.description: You must always construe a claim with reference to the whole context of a specification. Every claim in every patent must be read and construed with reference to the specification, and not as if the claim was an isolated sentence having no connection with or reference to what precedes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court authorities cited (Plimpton v. Spiller; Edison & Swan v. Woodhouse; Kaye v. Chubb). Read claims in light of specification to determine scope; do not treat claims in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior court interpretation binds later proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a specification has received an interpretation in the Court of Appeal and afterwards goes there again on appeal from the decision in another action against another defendant, the construction previously put upon it will be adopted and will not be allowed to be questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Automatic Weighing Machine Co. v. Combined Weighing Machine Co.; prior judicial construction should be followed in later cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous claim: prefer construction that does not enlarge monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim can be read in two senses, one of which would make the patentee appear to claim something which was well known and in common use, the construction should be such as not to enlarge the patentee's monopoly beyond what he is entitled to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Cropper v. Smith; Westinghouse v. Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Co.; Tindal in Haworth v. Hardcastle. Even if one construction makes claim practically repetitive of prior art, it will not invalidate patent provided it does not seek to enlarge monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making appendant claims to old matter
rubrics_metrics.description: An appendant claim to something old does not necessarily vitiate a patent but is inadvisable: if held to extend the patent it could invalidate it, and if held not to extend it the claim is useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: British Dynamite Co. v. Krebs. Inventors should avoid claiming known components as appendant claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition statutory time limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may, at any time within two months from the date of the advertisement of the acceptance of a complete specification give notice at the Patent Office of opposition to the grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory provision from s.11 of Patents Act 1883 (as amended). Strict two-month limit measured from advertisement of acceptance of complete specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted statutory grounds of opposition (three grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: An opponent is restricted to three grounds: (i) that the applicant had obtained the invention from him, or from a person of whom he is the legal representative; (ii) that the invention had been patented in this country on an application of prior date; or (iii) that the complete specification describes or claims an invention other than that described in the provisional specification, and that such other invention forms the subject of an application made by the opponent in the interval between the leaving of the provisional and the leaving of the complete specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the exclusive statutory grounds (Act of 1883, amended 1888). The third ground was substituted by s.4 Patents Act 1888.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition notice must state grounds and particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice of opposition must state the grounds of opposition. When the ground is that the invention has been previously patented, the title, number, and date of the alleged prior specification must be duly specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Patents Rules 1890, rules 34-44. Failure to state particulars limits what can be gone into at the hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence in opposition in form of statutory declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: The opponent's evidence in support of his case and the applicant's evidence in reply must be in the form of statutory declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal evidentiary requirement for proceedings before the Comptroller; follow rules for statutory declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing limited to matters in notice of opposition; amendments allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: At the hearing before the Comptroller no matter can be gone into which has not been stated in the notice of opposition. He may allow amendments in the notice of opposition at the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comptroller has discretion to permit amendment; but parties should ensure the notice is comprehensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onus of proof lies on the opponent
rubrics_metrics.description: At the hearing the parties may appear in person, or be represented by counsel, solicitors, or patent agents. The onus of proof lies on the opponent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case authority: Ex parte Sheffield, L. R. 8 Ch. 237. Opponent must prove his statutory ground(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller practice: favour applicant when doubt exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the law officer or Comptroller is in doubt as to the right to a patent, it is the well-recognised practice that the question should be determined in the applicant's favour and the patent sealed; law officers are reluctant to stop patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: Dance's Patent; Liddell's Patent; He Russell's Patent. Strongly contested scientific anticipation will not ordinarily cause the patent to be stopped — such matters can be tried in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to the law officer: notice within 14 days
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person intends to appeal to the law officer against the Comptroller's decision, he must file in the Patent Office a notice of his intention within fourteen days from the date of the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Rules of the Law Officers in the Appendix. Timing can be affected by amendments: the time for appealing may date from forwarding of approved amendment copy to the opponent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-appeal limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a notice of appeal is given by one party, the other party will not be allowed to question at the hearing another part of the Comptroller's decision unless he has also given notice of appeal, or has obtained the consent of the other side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Party who wishes to expand the scope of the appeal should file their own notice or obtain consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: First statutory ground: derived from opponent / legal representative — narrow interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The first ground is that the applicant had obtained the invention from the opponent, or from a person of whom he is the legal representative. A workman assisting his master in improving details of master's machine does not afford ground of opposition to the master's patent; an agent appointed by power of attorney does not fulfil 'legal representative'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Edmund's Patent; other authorities. The meaning of 'legal representative' is construed narrowly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second statutory ground: prior patent in this country — standing and particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The opponent must be a person who has a real interest in the prior patent, or the originator of the invention sought to be patented. Manufacturing under a prior patent is not necessarily sufficient; alleging intention to work is insufficient. A prior patent described but not claimed is not 'patented in this country'; provisional protection alone cannot be cited against applicant; however, a complete specification accepted at the Office (even if patent not issued) entitles the party to be heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Heath & Frost's Patent; Glossop's Patent; MacEvoy's Patent; Bailey's Patent; Paterson's Patent; L'Oiseau d'Pierrard. Provide title/number/date when relying on a prior patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim covered by earlier patent, applicant ordered to strike it out or insert disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it is clear that a claim is covered by an earlier patent the applicant will be ordered to strike it out. An applicant is frequently required to state in his specification that he is aware of a given patent and that he does not claim anything which is described and claimed in the specification under it; disclaimers are sometimes ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to an earlier specification must not put a construction on the later one. Cases: Hall & Hall; Webster; Grenfell & others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rival applications — joint grants, partitioning, and trusteeship
rubrics_metrics.description: When two contending applicants claim to be independent contemporaneous discoverers, the law officer usually refuses to allow the grant to issue to either separately but offers it to the two jointly. Where one applicant is entitled to part and the other to another part, warrants may be issued to both limiting specifications accordingly; patents have been ordered to be vested in trustees for the benefit of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Craig and Macfarlane; Evans & Cutting; cases where Lord Chancellor ordered different allocations or trusteeship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority and dating on sealing
rubrics_metrics.description: Under s.13 of the Act of 1883 every patent shall be dated and sealed as of the day of the application. Priority of sealing will not confer advantage: patent dated as of application day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical cases (Ex parte Bates & Redgate etc.) influenced practice; current rule: date is day of application regardless of sealing order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mala fides: court may interfere to prevent injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: If mala fides (bad faith) can be made out — e.g., a servant's invention appropriated by master — the Chancellor would interfere to prevent injustice and may order sealing and dating in favour of the true inventor; if the applicant derived the invention from a rival applicant the Seal may be refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ex parte Scott & Young; Hadden/Lott cartridge case; Macfarlane & colleagues. If invention was communicated in confidence and patentee obtained fraudulent patent, Lord Chancellor may direct sealing to permit court action. Law officers cannot take official notice of alleged foreign fraud against an opponent (Abel's Application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs: Comptroller vs law officers' powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comptroller has no authority to award costs; the law officers have power, under s.38 of the Act of 1883, to order costs to be paid by either party and any such order may be made a rule of Court. As a general rule costs follow the event, but special circumstances may influence the law officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Law Officers Rules 11 and 12. Frivolous oppositions should be ordered to pay applicant's costs where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sealing timing: patent sealed within 15 months (exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent shall be sealed as soon as may be, and not after the expiration of fifteen months from the date of application, except (1) where sealing has been delayed by an appeal to the law officer or by opposition to the grant, in which case the patent may be sealed at such time as the law officer may direct; and (2) if the applicant dies before expiration of the fifteen months, in which case the patent may be granted to his legal representative and sealed within twelve months of death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments (Act of 1885) allow limited extensions for complete specification and thereby permit up to four further months for sealing when extensions are allowed; applications for enlargement must state circumstances (Forms U and V).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent dated as of day of application; death of applicant provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent shall be dated and sealed as of the day of the application. If applicant dies before sealing the patent may be granted to legal representative and sealed within twelve months of death upon production of will/letters of administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure requires official copy or extract from will or letters of administration to prove legal representative's title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller may refuse grant if use contrary to law or morality
rubrics_metrics.description: By s.86 of the Patents Act 1883 the Comptroller may refuse to grant a patent for an invention the use of which would, in his opinion, be contrary to law or morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretionary public policy ground; exercise of this power is subject to administrative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial extent of a sealed patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent when sealed shall have effect throughout the United Kingdom and the Isle of Man, leaving out the Channel Islands which have been previously included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 16 of the Act of 1883 sets territorial effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent duration: fourteen years from its date
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration of every patent is limited to fourteen years from its date. Time runs from the day of the date of the patent, including that day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: patent dated Feb 26, 1825 expired at midnight Feb 25, 1839. Extensions / renewals discussed in later chapter (Chapter XIV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and unity of invention in patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent may be in the prescribed form; by statute a patent is to be granted for one invention only, but no objection to a patent can be taken in an action or other proceeding on the ground that it comprises more than one invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board of Trade has power to alter form. Section 33 of Act of 1888 reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisoes rendering grant void (non-payment, Crown supply)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two important provisoes make the grant void: (1) if the patentee does not pay all fees by law required at the times and in the manner provided; and (2) if the patentee does not supply or cause to be supplied for the service of the Crown all such articles of the invention as may be required by officers at reasonable prices and terms as settled by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to pay prescribed fees leads to cessation of patent (payments: 50L before end of fourth year and 100L before end of eighth year, or annual fees as set in Appendix). See Patents Rules 1890 rules 45-48 for certificates of payment/renewal.
